sourceDefinition: White; contr. of A^asowadu ; (A, K;) having whiteness: (Msb:) fem. bayoDaA='u : (Msb:) pl. biyDN , originally buyoDN , (S, Msb, K,) the damm being converted into kesr in order that the Y may remain unchanged, (S, K,) [i. e.] to suit the Y . (Msb.) In the phrase A^aEoTiniY A^aboyaD~aho , mentioned by Sb, as used by some of the Arabs, meaning A^aboyaDa , [i. e. Give thou to me a white one, ] h is subjoined as it is in hun~aho for hun~a , and the D is doubled because the letter of declinability cannot have h subjoined to it; wherefore the letter of declinability is the first D , and the second is the augmentative, and for this reason it has subjoined to it the h whereof the purpose is to render plainly perceivable the vowel [which is necessarily added after the doubled D ]: Aboo-'Alee says, [app. of the h ,] that it should properly have neither fet-h nor any vowel. (M.) ― -b2- Applied to a man &c., it was sometimes used to signify White in complexion: but in this sense they generally used the epithet A^aHomaru . (IAth, TA in art. Hmr .) They also said, fulaAnN A^aboyaDu Alwajohi and fulaAnapu bayoDaA='u Alwajohi , meaning Such a man, and such a woman, is clear, in face, from freckles or the like, and unseemly blackness. (Az, TA.) And they used biyDaAnN , (S, K,) a pl. of A^aboyaDu , (TA,) in the contr. of the sense of suwdaAnN , (S, K,) [i. e. as signifying Whites, ] applied to men: (S:) though they applied the appellation A^abuw AlbayoDaA='i to the Abyssinian: (TA in art. Ewr :) or to the negro: and A^abuw Aljawoni to the white man. (ISk.) But accord. to Th, A^aboyaDu applied to a man signifies only (tropical:) Pure; free from faults: (IAth, TA in art. Hmr :) or, so applied, unsullied in honour, nobility, or estimation; (Az, K;) free from faults; and generous: and so bayoDaA='u applied to a woman. (Az.) [In the lexicons, however, (see, for ex., among countless other instances, an explanation of baD~apN in the S,) and in other post-classical works, it is generally used, when thus applied, in its proper sense, of White; or fair in complexion. ] ― -b3- katiybapN bayoDaA='u An army, or a portion thereof, upon which the whiteness of the [ arms or armour of ] iron is apparent. (M.) ― -b4- And bayoDaA='u alone, [as a subst.,] A piece of paper [ without writing ]. (Har p. 311.) ― -b5- AlA^aboyaDu The sword: (S, A, K:) because of its whiteness: (TA:) pl. biyDN . (S.) ― -b6- Silver: (A, K:) because of its whiteness: like as gold is called AlA^aHomaru [because of its redness]. (TA.) ― -b7- The saliva ( rDAb ) of the mouth. (Ham p. 348.) ― -b8- A certain star in the margin of the milky way. (A, K.) ― -b9- AlbayoDaA='u The sun: because of its whiteness. (M.) ― -b10- Waste, or uncultivated, or uninhabited, land: (K, * TA: [in the CK AljirAbu is erroneously put for AlxaraAbu :]) opposed to Als~awodaA='u : because dead lands are white; and when planted, become black and green. (TA.) See also bayoDapN , near the end. ― -b11- Wheat: (K:) as also Als~amoraA='u . (TA.) ― -b12- Fresh [ grain of the kind called ] sulot . (El- Khattábee, K.) ― -b13- A certain kind of wood; that which is called AlHawaru : (K in art. Hwr :) because of its whiteness. (TA in that art.) [See HawarN .] ― -b14- The cooking-pot; as also A^um~u bayoDaA='a . (AA, K.) ― -b15- The snare with which one catches game. (IAar, K.) ― -b16- AlA^aboyaDaAni Milk and water. (ISk, S, M, A, K.) A poet says, wamaA liYa A_il~aA AlA^aboyaDayoni $araAbu [ And I have not any beverage except milk and water ]. (ISk, S, M.) ― -b17- Bread and water: (As, M, K:) or wheat and water: (Fr, K:) or fat and milk. (AO, K.) ― -b18- Fat and youthfulness (AZ, IAar, M, A, K.) You say, *ahaba A^aboyaDaAhu His fat and youthfulness departed. (TA.) ― -b19- maA raA^ayotuhu mu*o A^aboyaDaAni I have not seen him for, or during, two days: (Ks, M, A, K:) or two months. (Ks, M, K.) ― -b20- A^ay~aAmu AlbiyDi , (Msb, K,) or simply AlbiyDu , (Mgh,) for A^ay~aAmu All~ayaAliY AlbiyDi ; [ The days of the white nights; ] i. e. the days of the thirteenth and fourteenth and fifteenth nights of the month; (Mgh, Msb, K;) so called because they are lighted by the moon throughout: (Msb:) or of the twelfth and thirteenth and fourteenth nights: (K:) but this is of weak authority, and extr.: the former is the correct explanation: (MF, TA:) you should not say AlA^ay~aAmu AlbiyDu : (Ibn-El-Jawá- leekee, IB, K:) yet thus it is in most relations of a trad. in which it occurs; and some argue for it; and the author of the K has himself explained AlA^awaADiHu by AlA^ay~aAmu AlbiyDu . (TA.) ― -b21- sanapN bayoDaA='u (assumed tropical:) A year [ of scarcity of herbage, ] such as is a mean between that which is termed $ahobaA=' and that which is termed HamoraA=' . (TA in art. $hb .) ― -b22- kalaAmN A^aboyaDu (tropical:) Language expounded or explained. (M.) ― -b23- kal~amotuhu famaA rad~a EalaY~a sawodaA='a walaA bayoDaA='a (tropical:) I spoke to him, and he did not return to me a bad word nor a good one. (M.) ― -b24- yadN bayoDaA='u (assumed tropical:) A demonstrating, or demonstrated, argument, plea, allegation, or evidence. (M.) ― -b25- And (assumed tropical:) A favour, or benefit, for which one is not reproached; and which is conferred without its being asked. (M.) [See also yadN .] ― -b26- Almawotu AlA^aboyaDu (assumed tropical:) Sudden death; (K, TA;) such as is not preceded by disease which alters the complexion: or, as some say, death without the repentance, and the prayer for forgiveness, and the accomplishment of necessary duties, usual with him who is not taken unawares; from bay~aDa signifying “ he emptied ” a vessel: so says Sgh: opposed to Almawotu AlA^aHomaru , which is slaughter. (TA.) ― -b27- bayoDaA='u also signifies (assumed tropical:) A calamity, or misfortune: (Sgh, K:) app. as a term of good omen; like saliymN applied to one who is stung by a scorpion or bitten by a serpent. (TA.) ― -b28- bayoDaA='u AlqayoZi : see bayoDapN , last sentence but one. -A2- h`*aA A^aboyaDu mino ka*aA ; &c.: see bayaADN .

sourceDefinition: He watered camels to their satisfaction: (S, M, K; but in some copies of the S, the verb is made trans. by means of bi :) or he watered them (T, M) so as to quench their thirst, (T,) but not so as to satisfy them. definition: A receptacle, such as when one folds the skirt of his shirt and puts in it a thing and carries it before him: (S:) or the part, of the garment, which is the place wherein one carries, when he wraps...
sourceDefinition: A receptacle, such as when one folds the skirt of his shirt and puts in it a thing and carries it before him: (S:) or the part, of the garment, which is the place wherein one carries, when he wraps it around his body, or puts a portion thereof under his right shoulder and another portion over his left shoulder, then folds before him a part of it, and puts a thing in it; as also ↓ vubonapN : (M:) or the part, of one's garment, which is the place wherein he carries; folding its extremity, and sewing it, before him, and then putting in it some dates or other things: as also ↓ vabiynN and ↓ vubonapN : (K:) and the extremity of the [ garment called ] ridaA=' when one folds it before him and sews it [ and puts a thing in it to carry ]: (M:) or a receptacle in which one carries a thing before him; (T:) and ↓ vubonapN , of which the pl. is vubaAnN , (T,) or its pl. is vubanN , like as the pl of xubonapN [which has a similar meaning] is xubanN , (Har p. 427,) the doubled upper border of the trousers or waist-wrapper, in which one carries [ before him ] fruit and other things: [see also xubonapN :] or, as some say, vibaAnN does not signify a receptacle, but dates that are put and carried in a receptacle or some other thing: and sometimes what a man carries in his sleeve; and ↓ vubonapN signifies only what one carries before him, that is little in quantity: and what is great is not called vibaAnN . (T.) It is said in a trad. of 'Omar, A_i*aA mar~a A^aHadukumo biHaAy^iTK faloyaA^okulo minohu walaA yat~axi*o vibaAnFA [ When any one of you passes by a garden of palm-trees, let him eat thereof, but not take for himself, or make, a vbAn ]: i. e., when a necessitous hungry person passes by a man's garden of palm-trees, he may eat of their dates what will repel his hunger. (T. [See also another reading voce xubonapN .]) And one says, qadima fulaAnN bivibaAnK fiY vawobihi maA A^adoriY maA huwa [ Such a one came with a vbAn in his garment: I know not what it was ]. (T.)

sourceDefinition: [ Garlic; the allium sativum of Linn.;] a kind of baqol , (AHn, M,) well known, (S,) abundant in the country of the Arabs; (AHn, M;) of two sorts; wild, (AHn, M, K,) and growing in the cultivated tracts, (AHn, M,) or in gardens: (K:) the former sort is called vuwmu AlHay~api , and is the stronger, (K,) and is brought from Syria: (TA:) each of them is heating, expels flatulence and worms, and is strongly diuretic; and this is the most excellent [ property ] that is therein: it is good for obliviousness, and asthma, and chronic cough, and [ pain in ] the spleen and the flank, and colic, and sciatica, &c.: (K: [in which are added many other supposed uses:]) n. un. with p . (AHn, M, K.) ― -b2- Hence, as being likened thereto, (M,) vuwmapN signifies also (tropical:) The pommel of a sword. (S, M, K.) Whence, A^um~u vuwomapa , said to be the name of a certain woman, may mean (tropical:) A sword. (M.) ― -b3- [Hence, also,] vuwomapu *akari rajulK (assumed tropical:) [ The glans of a man's penis ]. (Az, in TA voce TurovuwvN .) ― -b4- Alv~uwmapu also signifies The channel [or oblong depression ] between the two mustaches, against the partition between the two nostrils; (IAar, TA;) i. q. AlxunoEubapu , &c. (TA in art. xnEb .) -A2- vuwmN is also a dial. var. of fuwmN , meaning Wheat. (Lh, T, M.) And the latter is used in the [ordinary] sense of the former. (T.)

See also 1, last sentence but one.

Also (assumed tropical:) God's particular, or peculiar, distinguishing of men by abundant bounty, from which various blessings result to them without their labour; as happens to prophets and some others. (Er-Rághib, TA.)

Also AjtbAhu , (assumed tropical:) He forged it: and he extemporized it. (TA.) Hence, in the Kur [vii. 202], qaAluwA lawolaA A@jotabayotahaA (assumed tropical:) They say, Wherefore hast thou not forged it, (Fr, TA,) or produced it, (Th, TA,) or invented it, (Jel,) or put it together by forgery, (Bd,) of thyself? (Fr, Th, Bd, Jel, TA:) or wherefore hast thou not sought it, or demanded it, of God? (Bd.)

sourceDefinition: , or jabFY , (as in different copies of the K,) written with A and with Y , (TA,) The camel-waterer's going in advance of the camels a day before their coming to the water, and collecting for them water in the drinking-trough, and then bringing them to it (IAar, K, TA) on the morrow. (IAar, TA.) [App. an inf. n., of which, in this sense, the verb is not mentioned.] So in the verse, biAlr~ayovi maA A^arowayotuhaA laA biAlEajalo wabiAljabaA A^arowayotuhaA laA biAlqabalo [ Slowly I satisfied their thirst; not hastily: and by going in advance of them a day, and collecting for them water in the trough, and bringing them to it on the morrow, I satisfied their thirst; not by pouring the water into the trough while they were drinking, without having prepared any for them beforehand ]. (IAar, TA.) -A2- Also the former, Water collected [in a trough ]; and so ↓ jubowapN , with damm. (TA. [See jibFA .]) ― -b2- A wateringtrough (K, TA) in which water is collected: (TA:) or the station of the drawer of water, upon the [upper part of the] casing. (K.) ― -b3- The place where a well is dug: (K:) in this sense, and in the next, also written jabFY (TA.) ― -b4- The brink, or margin, of a well. (A boo-Leylà, K.) The earth that is around a well, that is seen from afar; (S;) originally jabaA^N : (TA:) what is around a well: (K:) and what is around a wateringtrough: (TA:) pl. A^ajobaA='N . (K.) -A3- jabaA meaning A gift without compensation is a vulgar word. (TA.)

definition: A beast (Lth, Mgh) before the vaniY~ [q.
sourceDefinition: A beast (Lth, Mgh) before the vaniY~ [q. v.], (Lth, S, Mgh, Msb, K,) by one year; when it may for the first time be ridden and used: (Lth:) fem. with p : (S, Mgh, Msb, K:) pl. masc. [of pauc.] A^jo*aAEN (Yoo, O) and [of mult.] ju*oEaAnN (Yoo, S, Mgh, Msb, K) and ji*oEaAnN (L, Msb) and ji*aAEN (S, Mgh, Msb, K) and ju*aAEN ; (Yoo, O;) and pl. fem. ja*aEaAtN : (S, Msb:) it is a name applied to the beast in a particular time, not denoting a tooth growing or falling out: (S, K:) but it differs in its application to different kinds of beasts: (Az:) applied to a sheep or goat, it means a year old; (IAar;) in his second year: (Mgh:) or, applied to a sheep, a year old; and sometimes less than a year, by reason of plenty of food; (IAar;) or eight months old, (Az, Mgh, TA,) or nine; (TA;) or, when from young parents, from six months old to seven; and when from very old parents from eight months old to ten; (IAar, Mgh;) and the sheep thus called is a satisfactory victim for sacrifice: (Mgh, TA:) and applied to a goat, a year old; (Az, Mgh;) or in its second year; (AZ;) but the goat thus called is not a satisfactory victim for sacrifice: (Mgh:) applied to a bull, it means in like manner in his second year; (Mgh;) or in his third year; and the bull thus called is not a satisfactory victim for sacrifice: (TA:) applied to a horse, it means in his third year; (IAar;) or in his fourth year: (Mgh:) [but see qaAriHN :] and applied to a camel, in his fifth year; (Az, Mgh;) fem. with p ; and this (a j*Ep ) is what must be given for the poor-rate when the camels are more than sixty. (Az, TA.) [See also $aSarN .] ― -b2- A youth, or young man. (K.) ― -b3- (assumed tropical:) One who is light-witted, or weak and stupid, like a youth: opposed in this sense to baAzilN as meaning “ old: ” (IAar, TA:) or one whose teeth have fallen out, here and there, [as though likened to a beast thus termed that has shed some of his first teeth,] because he has drawn near to his appointed term of life. (TA: [but it is not quite clear whether this explanation relate to j*E or to bAzl .]) ― -b4- (tropical:) [ A novice, or recent beginner. ] You say, fulaAnN fiY h`*aA AlA^amori ja*aEN (tropical:) [ Such a one, in this affair, is a novice, or recent beginner, ] when he has begun it recently. (S, Z.) ― -b5- Ald~ahoru ja*aEN A^abadFA (tropical:) Time, or fortune, is ever new, like a youth. (K, * TA.) ― -b6- Hence, (TA,) AlA^azolamu Alja*aEu (tropical:) Time, or fortune; (S, K;) as in the saying, A^aholakahumu AlA^azolamu Alja*aEu (tropical:) Time, or fortune, destroyed them; and laA A=tiyka AlA^azolama Alja*aEa (tropical:) I will not come to thee ever. (TA.) [See also art. zlm .] And accord. to some, (S,) The lion: (S, K:) but this is a mistake. (IB, L.) ― -b7- And hence, (TA,) A^um~u Alja*aEi (tropical:) Calamity, or misfortune. (K, TA.) ― -b8- A^aEadotu AlA^amora ja*aEFA (tropical:) I renewed the thing, or affair, as it was at the first: as, for instance, a war which had been extinguished. (TA.) And far~a AlA^amora ja*aEFA [signifies, in like manner, (tropical:) He recommenced the thing: or] he commenced the thing. (TA.) And fur~a AlA^amoru ja*aEFA (tropical:) The thing was commenced: (TA:) or the thing returned to its first state; it recommenced. (K in art. fr .) ― -b9- ju*oEaAnu AljibaAli (assumed tropical:) Small mountains. (K.)

[of pauc.] A^jo*aAEN (Yoo, O) and [of mult.] ju*oEaAnN (Yoo, S, Mgh, Msb, K) and ji*oEaAnN (L, Msb) and ji*aAEN (S, Mgh, Msb, K) and ju*aAEN ; (Yoo, O;) and pl. fem. ja*aEaAtN : (S, Msb:) it is a name applied to the beast in a particular time, not denoting a tooth growing or falling out: (S, K:) but it differs in its application to different kinds of beasts: (Az:) applied to a sheep or goat, it means a year old; (IAar;) in his second year: (Mgh:) or, applied to a sheep, a year old; and sometimes less than a year, by reason of plenty of food; (IAar;) or eight months old, (Az, Mgh, TA,) or nine; (TA;) or, when from young parents, from six months old to seven; and when from very old parents from eight months old to ten; (IAar, Mgh;) and the sheep thus called is a satisfactory victim for sacrifice: (Mgh, TA:) and applied to a goat, a year old; (Az, Mgh;) or in its second year; (AZ;) but the goat thus called is not a satisfactory victim for sacrifice: (Mgh:) applied to a bull, it means in like manner in his second year; (Mgh;) or in his third year; and the bull thus called is not a satisfactory victim for sacrifice: (TA:) applied to a horse, it means in his third year; (IAar;) or in his fourth year: (Mgh:) [but see qaAriHN :] and applied to a camel, in his fifth year; (Az, Mgh;) fem. with p ; and this (a j*Ep ) is what must be given for the poor-rate when the camels are more than sixty. (Az, TA.) [See also $aSarN .] ― -b2- A youth, or young man. (K.) ― -b3- (assumed tropical:) One who is light-witted, or weak and stupid, like a youth: opposed in this sense to baAzilN as meaning “ old: ” (IAar, TA:) or one whose teeth have fallen out, here and there, [as though likened to a beast thus termed that has shed some of his first teeth,] because he has drawn near to his appointed term of life. (TA: [but it is not quite clear whether this explanation relate to j*E or to bAzl .]) ― -b4- (tropical:) [ A novice, or recent beginner. ] You say, fulaAnN fiY h`*aA AlA^amori ja*aEN (tropical:) [ Such a one, in this affair, is a novice, or recent beginner, ] when he has begun it recently. (S, Z.) ― -b5- Ald~ahoru ja*aEN A^abadFA (tropical:) Time, or fortune, is ever new, like a youth. (K, * TA.) ― -b6- Hence, (TA,) AlA^azolamu Alja*aEu (tropical:) Time, or fortune; (S, K;) as in the saying, A^aholakahumu AlA^azolamu Alja*aEu (tropical:) Time, or fortune, destroyed them; and laA A=tiyka AlA^azolama Alja*aEa (tropical:) I will not come to thee ever. (TA.) [See also art. zlm .] And accord. to some, (S,) The lion: (S, K:) but this is a mistake. (IB, L.) ― -b7- And hence, (TA,) A^um~u Alja*aEi (tropical:) Calamity, or misfortune. (K, TA.) ― -b8- A^aEadotu AlA^amora ja*aEFA (tropical:) I renewed the thing, or affair, as it was at the first: as, for instance, a war which had been extinguished. (TA.) And far~a AlA^amora ja*aEFA [signifies, in like manner, (tropical:) He recommenced the thing: or] he commenced the thing. (TA.) And fur~a AlA^amoru ja*aEFA (tropical:) The thing was commenced: (TA:) or the thing returned to its first state; it recommenced. (K in art. fr .) ― -b9- ju*oEaAnu AljibaAli (assumed tropical:) Small mountains. (K.)

sourceDefinition: , (S, K,) aor. , (TA,) inf. n. ja*owN and ju*uw~N , (K,) It (a thing, TA) stood firmly; as also ↓ Aj*Y . (S, K.) You say also, ja*aA EalaY $aYo'K He [or it, for instance, a stone of those (three in number) upon which a cooking-pot is places, as is implied in the S, (see jaA*K ,)] remained firm upon a thing. (S.) And ja*aA AlquraAdu fiY janobi AlbaEiyr The ticks stuck, and clave, to the side of the camel: (ISd, K, TA:) and j*A biAljamali clung to the camel. (TA.) ― -b2- I. q. javFA [ He sat upon his knees; &c.]; (AA, Fr, S, K;) as also ↓ Aijo*awaY , [in form] like AiroEawaY ; (TA;) except that j*A is more indicative of keeping to a place: (Kh, TA:) or he stood upon the extremities of his toes: (As, K:) accord. to Th, ju*uw~N is [the standing ] upon the extremities of the toes; and juvuw~N is [the sitting] upon the knees: (TA:) and accord. to IAar, ↓ jaA*K means [a man standing ] upon his feet; and jaAvK , [one sitting] upon his knees. (S, TA.) Accord. to El-Hasan Ibn-'AbdAllah El-Kátib El-Isbahánee, ja*aA , inf. n. ju*uw~N , said of a bird, means He stood upon the extremities of his toes, and warbled, and went round in his warbling; which he does only when seeking the female: and said of a horse, it means he stood upon his toes; and in like manner when said of a man, whether for dancing or for some other purpose. (TA.) A poet says, (S,) namely, En-Noamán Ibn-Nadleh, (TA,) A_i*aA $iy^otu gan~atoniY dahaAqiynu qaroyapK waSan~aAjapN tajo*uw EalaY Harofi manosimi [ When I will, the husbandmen of a village sing to me, and a female player with the cymbals, standing upon the extremity of a toe ]. (S, TA: but in the latter, EalaY kul~i manosimi [ upon every toe ].) ― -b3- Also, inf. n. ju*uw~N , He, or it, was, or became, erect, and straight; (TA;) and so ↓ Aijo*awo*aY , inf. n. Aijo*iy*aA='N . (Az, TA.) See jawaA*i as applied to she-camels, in two places, voce jaA*K . ― -b4- It (a camel's hump) bore fat [ so that it became elevated ]. (K.) ― -b5- ja*aA manoxiraAhu His nostrils were, or became, raised and extended. (TA.) ― -b6- Er-Rá'ee, describing a strong, or sturdy, she-camel, says, lamo yajo*u mirofaquhaA fiY Ald~afi mino zawari meaning Her elbow did not stand out far from the side by reason of [ the distortion termed ] zawar . (TA.)

(TA.)

definition: The anterior [or under ] part of the neck of a camel, from his ma*obaH [or the part a little below the under jaw ] to the place where he is stabbed: (S, Msb, K:) and in like manner, of a horse;
sourceDefinition: The anterior [or under ] part of the neck of a camel, from his ma*obaH [or the part a little below the under jaw ] to the place where he is stabbed: (S, Msb, K:) and in like manner, of a horse; (S, TA;) the inner [or under ] part of the neck, from the pit of the uppermost part of the breast to the extremity of the neck at the head: and, metaphorically, of a man: (TA:) pl. [of mult.] jurunN (S, Msb, K) and [of pauc.] A^ajorinapN ; (Msb, TA;) which last is used by Tarafeh as a sing. (TA, * and EM p. 68.) See another ex. voce jironN . [And see a verse cited in the first paragraph of art. Hnw .] You say also, Daraba AlHaq~u bijiraAnihi , meaning (assumed tropical:) The truth, or right, or just claim, became established, or settled. (T, TA.) ― -b2- Also The inner [or under ] part of the penis: pl. jurunN and A^ajorinapN , as above. (TA.)

definition: What one has ground [of grain]: (K, TA:) of the dial.
sourceDefinition: What one has ground [of grain]: (K, TA:) of the dial. of Hudheyl. You say also, fulaAnN ↓ yatajas~ama AlmajaAsima and yataja$~amu AlmajaA$ima (tropical:) [app. meaning Such a one undertakes, in spite of difficulty or trouble or inconvenience, those things, or affairs, that are causes of difficulty or trouble or inconvenience; i. e., difficult, or troublesome, or inconvenient things or affairs: supposing the two nouns to be pls. of which the sings. are majosamapN and majo$amapN , of the measure mafoEalapN , like maboxalapN and majobanapN and ma$~aqapN (originally ma$oqaqapN ) &c.]. (TA.)

definition: The body, with the limbs or members;
sourceDefinition: The body, with the limbs or members; syn. jasadN ; (AZ, S, Msb;) as also ↓ jusomaAnN and juvomaAnN : (AZ, S, Msb: *) or jisomN and ↓ jusomaAnN are syn. with jasadN ; (As, S;) or signify the whole body and limbs or members of a man, (K, and T and Msb in explanation of jsm ,) and of a beast, a camel, and the like, (T, Msb,) and of any other species, (K,) of large make; (T, Msb, K;) and juvomaAnN is syn. with $axoSN [app. as meaning “ a person ”]; and ↓ jusomaAnN signifies the whole jisom of a man: (As, S:) or jisomN signifies [ a body, or material substance; a solid; ] a thing having length and breadth and thickness; so that, when it is cut and divided, no portion thereof ceases to be a jisom ; whereas a $axoS [meaning “ a person ”] ceases to be a $axoS by its being divided: (Er-Rághib, TA:) a thing that is capable of being divided in length and breadth and thickness is called jisomN TabiyEiY~N , and also, because it is a subject of investigation, or inquiry, in instruction in the mathematical studies, jisomN taEoliymiY~N : (KT:) pl. [of pauc.] A^ajosaAmN and [of mult] jusuwmN . (K.) You say, vaAba jisomuhu , (M, A, K, in art. vwb ,) and A^avaAba jisomuhu , (IKt, M, ib.,) and vaAba A_ilayohi jisomuhu , (T, M, A, ib.,) (tropical:) He became fat, after leanness; (A;) his good state of body returned to him; (M, K; *) his condition of body became good, after extenuation; and health, or soundness, thereof returned to him. (T.) And ↓ A_in~ahu laHaniyfu AljusomaAni [ Verily he is slender, spare, or lean, of body ]. (TA.) ― -b2- AlA^ajosaAmu Almuxotalifapu AlT~abaAy^iEi [ The material substances of different natures; also called AlA^ajosaAmu Als~aboEapu the seven material substances, and Alfili*aAtu ; namely,] the EanaASir [which are the four elements, fire, air, earth, and water, ] and the three products composed of these, (KT,) which are minerals, vegetables, and animals. (Note in a copy of the KT.) AlA^ajosaAmu AlT~abiyEiy~ahu , as used by those who study to discover occult things, signifies The Earo$ and the kurosiY~ : and AlA^ajosaAmu AlEunoSuriy~apu , everything beside these two, of the heavens and the [ elements termed ] A^usoTuqusaAt therein. (KT.)

definition: , (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K,) aor. and , (S, Msb, K,) inf. n. jalobN (S, Mgh, Msb, K) and jalabN , (S, K,) He drove, (A, K,) or brought, conveyed, or transported, (Mgh,) a thing, (S, A, * Mgh, Msb, K, *) or things, such as camels, sheep, goats, horses, captives, or slaves, or any merchandise, (TA,) from one place to another, (A, K,) or from one country or town to another, for the purpose of traffic; (Mgh;) as also ↓ Ajtlb , (A, K, KL,) and ↓ Astjlb . (KL.) And jalabotu Al$~aYo'a A_ilay nafosiY and ↓ Aijotalabotuhu signify the same; (S;) i. e. (assumed tropical:) I brought, drew, attracted, or procured, the thing to myself. (PS.) [Hence,] *aA mim~aA yajolibu AlA_ixowaAna (tropical:) [ This is of the things that bring, draw, attract, or procure, brothers, or friends ]. (A, TA.) And Ald~ahori ↓ jalabatuhu jawaAlibu (tropical:) [ The calamities of time, or of fortune, or of fate, brought, drew, or attracted, him, or it ]. (A, TA.) [Hence also, accord. to some,] laA jalaba wa laA janaba , a trad., explained as meaning, The owner of cattle shall not be required to drive them, or bring them, to the town, or country, in order that the collector may take from them the portion appointed for the poor-rate, but this shall be taken at the waters; and when the cattle are in the yards, they shall be left therein, and not brought forth to the place of pasture, for the collector to take that portion: or, as some say, wlA jnb means, nor shall one have a horse led by his side, in a race, in order that, when he draws near to the goal, he may tranfser himself to it, and so outstrip his fellow: and other explanations have been given: (Msb:) [accord. to some,] lA jlb here means, they shall not drive, or bring, their cattle to the collector of the portions appointed for the poor-rate in the place where he alights, but he shall himself come to their yards and take those portions: or [ jlb here is from the verb jalaba in a sense which will be explained below, and] the trad. relates to horse-racing, and means, one shall not cause his horse to be followed by a man crying out at it and chiding it; nor shall he have a horse without a rider led by his own horse, in order that, when he draws near to the goal, he may transfer himself to it, and outstrip upon it: (Mgh:) or Aljalabu , which is forbidden, means the collector's not coming to the people at their waters to take the portions appointed for the poor-rate, but ordering them to drive, or bring, their cattle to him: or it relates to contending for a stake, or wager, and means the mounting a man upon one's horse, and, when he has drawn near to the goal, following his horse and crying out at it, in order that it may outstrip; which is a kind of fraud: (S:) or it is used in both these cases: (A 'Obeyd: [his explanations are virtually the same as those in the S:]) or the meaning of the trad. [so far as the former clause of it is concerned] is, that the contributions to the poor-rate shall not be driven, or brought, to the waters nor to the great towns, but shall be given in their places of pasture: or it means, [or rather Aljlb means,] the collector's alighting in a place, and then sending a person, or persons, to drive, or bring, to him the cattle from their places, that he may take the portion thereof appointed for the poor-rate: or it [relates to horse-racing, and] means the sending forth a horse in the racecourse, and a number of persons' congregating, and crying out at it, in order that it may be turned from its course: or a man's following his horse, and spurring on behind it, and chiding it, and crying out at it: (K, TA:) or the shaking a thing behind a horse that is backward in a race, that it may be urged on thereby, and outstrip: or one's riding a horse, and leading behind him another, to urge it on, in contending for a stake, or wager: or the crying out at a horse from behind, and urging it to outstrip. (TA. See also 1 in art. jnb .) ― -b2- jalaba lA^aholihi He gained or earned; sought or sought after or sought to gain [provisions &c.; generally meaning he purveyed ]; and exercised art or cunning or skill, in the management of his affairs; for his family; as also ↓ Ajlb . (Lh, K.) -A2- jalabuwA , aor. and , (K,) [inf. n. jalabN , and perhaps jalabapN also;] and ↓ jl~bwA ; (S, K;) and ↓ AjlbwA , (K,) inf. n. A_ijolaAbN ; (Mgh;) [the second of which is the most common;] They raised cries, shouts, noises, a clamour, (S, Mgh, TA,) or confused cries or shouts or noises. (Mgh, K. *) And jalaba Ealay farasihi , (S, Msb, K,) aor. , (S, Msb,) inf. n. jalabN , (S,) or jalobN , (Msb,) He chid, or urged on, his horse; as also ↓ jl~b and ↓ Ajlb ; (K;) the first, rare; the second and third, usual: (TA:) he cried out at his horse, (S, K,) from behind him, and urged him to outstrip [ in a race ], (S,) aor. and ; (K; but this explanation is erased in the copy of the K in its author's handwriting, as being a repetition; and rightly, accord. to MF; though this requires consideration; TA;) as also ↓ Ajlb : (S:) he urged his horse to run, by striking, or goading, or by crying out, or the like; as also ↓ Ajlb : or, as some say, he led behind his horse that he was riding another horse to urge on the former, in contending [in a race] for a stake, or wager; as is shown in an explanation of the tradition cited above, laA jalaba walaA janaba . (TA.) It is said in the Kur [xvii. 66], Ealayohimo bixayolika warajolika ↓ waA^ajolibo And raise thou confused cries against them, (Mgh,) or cry out against them, with thy forces riding and on foot. (Bd. But see another explanation in what follows.) And it is said in a wellknown prov., jalabato jalobapF vum~a A^amosakato It, i. e. a cloud ( saHaAbap ), thundered, then refrained from raining: applied to a coward, who threatens, and then is silent: but accord. to some, it is with H in the place of j (MF. See art. Hlb .) ― -b2- [Hence,] jalaba , aor. and ; and ↓ Ajlb ; He threatened with evil; (K, TA;) followed by an accus. (TA) [or, app., by EalaY before the object]: or (so in the TA, but in some copies of the K “ and, ”) he collected a company, a troop, or an army. (K, TA.) [It is said that] Ealayohimo ↓ waA^ajolibo , in the Kur [xvii. 66], means And collect thou against them [ thy forces ], and threaten them with evil. (TA. But see another explanation above.) And Ealayohi ↓ Ajlbw signifies also They collected themselves together against him, (S, K, *) and aided one another; like AHlbwA . (S.) ― -b3- jalaba Ealayohi , aor. , inf. n. jalobN , He committed a crime against him; or an offence for which he should be punished. (K, * TA.) -A3- jalaba , aor. and , (S, K,) It (a wound) healed: (K:) or it (an ulcer, As, or a wound, S) became covered with a skin in healing: (As, S:) as also ↓ Ajlb . (S, L.) ― -b2- And It (blood) dried; became dry; as also ↓ Ajlb . (Lh, K.) -A4- jaliba , aor. , It [app. a company or troop] assembled, or became collected together. (K.)

[so far as the former clause of it is concerned] is, that the contributions to the poor-rate shall not be driven, or brought, to the waters nor to the great towns, but shall be given in their places of pasture: or it means, [or rather Aljlb means,] the collector's alighting in a place, and then sending a person, or persons, to drive, or bring, to him the cattle from their places, that he may take the portion thereof appointed for the poor-rate: or it [relates to horse-racing, and] means the sending forth a horse in the racecourse, and a number of persons' congregating, and crying out at it, in order that it may be turned from its course: or a man's following his horse, and spurring on behind it, and chiding it, and crying out at it: (K, TA:) or the shaking a thing behind a horse that is backward in a race, that it may be urged on thereby, and outstrip: or one's riding a horse, and leading behind him another, to urge it on, in contending for a stake, or wager: or the crying out at a horse from behind, and urging it to outstrip. Hence the prov., Aln~ufaADu yuqaT~iru Aljalaba The failure of provisions causes the camels, driven, or brought, from one place to another, to be disposed in files for sale. (TA.) ― -b2- [And, app., Male camels; like jaluwbapN ; because they are driven, or brought, from one place to another, and sold; (see 4;) opposed to HalabN , q. v.] ― -b3- Also Persons who drive, or bring, camels and sheep or goats [ &c. ] from one place or country or town to another, for sale; and so [its pl.] A^ajolaAbN . (S.) [In the present day, ↓ jal~aAbN signifies One who brings slaves from foreign countries, particularly from African countries, for sale. ] -A2- Also, (S, A, K,) and ↓ jalabapN , (S, A, * Mgh, K,) [the former an inf. n., and so, perhaps, the latter, but often used as simple substs., the latter more commonly, meaning] Cries, shouts, noises, or clamour: (S, TA:) or a confusion, or mixture, (A, Mgh, K,) of cries or shouts or noises, (A, Mgh,) or of crying or shouting or noise. (K.) ― -b2- And the former, An assembly of men. (TA.)

definition: The small piece of skin, (S,) or the crust, or scab, (A, K,) that forms over a wound (S, A, K) when it heals: (S, K:) pl.

definition: A xazarap [i. e. bead, or gem, or similar stone ] (T, K, TA) used by the Arabs of the desert, (T, TA,) [or by the women of the desert, as a charm, ] for captivating, or fascinating, men; (K, * TA;)...
sourceDefinition: A xazarap [i. e. bead, or gem, or similar stone ] (T, K, TA) used by the Arabs of the desert, (T, TA,) [or by the women of the desert, as a charm, ] for captivating, or fascinating, men; (K, * TA;) or for bringing back after flight; (T, K;) or for procuring affection after hatred: (T, TA:) Az mentions it as a quadriliteral-radical word. (TA.) The Arab women used to say, falaA yarumo walaA yagibo A^ax~a*otuhu biAlyanojalibo walaA yazilo Einoda AlT~anabo [ I have fascinated him with the yenjelib, and he shall not seek another, nor absent himself, nor cease to remain at the tent-rope ]. (Lh, TA.)

definition: i. q. qaSorN [ A palace: or a pavilion, or kind of building wholly or for the most. part isolated, sometimes on the top of a larger building, i. e., a belvedere, and sometimes projecting from a...
sourceDefinition: i. q. qaSorN [ A palace: or a pavilion, or kind of building wholly or for the most. part isolated, sometimes on the top of a larger building, i. e., a belvedere, and sometimes projecting from a larger building, and generally consisting of one room if forming a part of a larger building ]: (S, K, and Ham p. 823:) or a fortress; syn. HiSonN : (M, IB, TA:) or [ a building ] resembling a HiSon : (M:) an arabicized word, (Lth, JK, S, M,) from the Persian kuw$ok : (TA:) its primary meaning is a HiSon in a state of demolition; and a ruined qaSor : pl. jawaAsiqu and jawaAsiyqu ; the latter formed by giving fulness of sound to the kesreh, or by poetic license. (Ham ubi suprà.) There were, in the Karáfeh, [the great burial-ground of the Egyptian metropolis,] numerous quSuwr , i. e., what are called jwAsq , having belvederes ( manaAZir ) and gardens: but most of the jwAsq were without gardens and without a well; being lofty belvederes: all of them were called quSuwr . (El-Makreezee's “ Khitat, ” ii. 453.)

definition: Rank, station, or dignity, (S, K, TA, and JK in art.
sourceDefinition: Rank, station, or dignity, (S, K, TA, and JK in art. wjh ,) with, or in the estimation of, the Sultán; (JK, TA;) as also ↓ jaAhapN , (K,) on the authority of Lh, (TA, as from the K, [but not in my copies,]) or, accord. to Sgh, of Ks.: the former word [probably arabicized from the Persian jaAho ; but] said to be formed by transposition from wajohN ; this being first changed to jawohN ; then, to jawahN ; and then, to jaAhN : or, accord. to Lh, it is not from wajohN , but from juhot [app. juhotu , first pers. sing. of jaAha , q. v.]; though he does not explain what is juhot . (TA.) You say, fulaAnN *uw jaAhK [ Such a one is possessed of rank, station, or dignity ]. (S.) And lifulaAnK jaAhN fiyhimo To such a one belongs rank, station, or dignity, among them. (Aboo-Bekr, TA.) The dim. of jaAhN [or of jaAhapN ] is ↓ juwayohapN . (TA.) -A2- jaAhi , indecl., with kesr for its termination; and, accord. to As, sometimes, jaAhK , with tenween; (S;) or jaAhi jaAhi , (JK, K,) and jaAhK jaAhK , and jaAho jaAho , (Lh, K,) and juwh ↓ juwh , or jawoh jawoh , (accord. to different copies of the K, but) indecl., with kesr for the termination, [i. e. juwhi juwhi , or jawohi jawohi ,] mentioned in the M, (TA,) and ↓ jaAhi laA jihota , (IDrd, TA, [see 1,]) ejaculations used for chiding a he-camel, not a she-camel: (As, JK, IDrd, S, K:) or one says to a she-camel, EaAjK and jaAhK . (A 'Obeyd, TA in art. Ewj : [or perhaps there is an omission here: I think it more likely that what A 'Obeyd said was that one says to a she-camel EaAjK , and to a he-camel jaAhK .])

definition: , (S, Msb, TA,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, Msb, TA,) aor. , (Msb,) inf. n. HaborN ; (S, Msb, TA;) and ↓ Hb~rhu , (TA,) inf. n. taHobyrN ; (S, K, TA;) or the latter has an intensive signification; (Msb;) He made it beautiful, beautified it, (S, K, TA,) or adorned it, or embellished it, (Msb,) and made it plain; (TA;) namely, handwriting, and poetry, &c., (S, K, both in relation to the latter verb, and TA in relation to both verbs,) such as language, or speech, and science, (S, TA,) and pronunciation, and a recitation; meaning, with respect to the last, the voice [with which he recited]. (TA.) ― -b2- Also Habarahu , (S, A, L, Msb, but in the Msb “ or, ” not “ also, ”) aor. , inf. n. HaborN (S, Msb) and HaborapN ; (S;) and ↓ AHbrhu ; (K;) and in an intensive sense ↓ Hb~rhu ; (Msb;) He, (God, A,) or it, (a thing, or an affair or event, S, L,) made him happy, joyful, or glad; (S, A, L, Msb, K;) affected him with a happiness, joy, or gladness, that made his face to shine, or of which the mark, or sign, ( HabaAr , i. e. A^avar ,) appeared upon his countenance; (Bd in xliii. 70, in explanation of the pass. form of the first of these verbs;) he made him to enjoy a state of ease and plenty; and treated him with honour: (Lth and S in explanation of the pass. form of the first verb as used in the Kur xxx. 14:) or treated him with extraordinary honour. (Bd in xliii. 70, and TA.) [ Hubira , properly signifying He was made happy, &c., may be used as meaning he was, or became, happy, &c.; like sur~a ; and HubuwrN , and its syns. mentioned with it below, may be regarded as its inf. ns. Golius, app. from his finding HabarN explained in the KL as an inf. n. meaning The being happy, &c., ( $aAdo $udano ,) assigns to Hubira jiloduhu , as on the authority of that lexicon, the meaning of “ hilaris lætusque fuit; ” but I have not found this verb in any Arabic work.] -A2- Hubira jiloduhu His skin was beaten so that there remained the mark of the beating. (K.) -A3- Habira AljuroHu , (S, K,) aor. , (K,) inf. n. HabarN , (S,) The wound broke out afresh: (S, K:) or became healed, but left scars. (Ks, S, K.) ― -b2- Habrato A^asonaAnuhu , aor. , (S, A, * Msb, K,) inf. n. HabarN , (S, Msb, *) His teeth became of a yellow colour mingled with the whiteness: (K:) or became yellow; (A, Msb;) syn. qaliHato . (S.) [See also HibirN .]

sourceDefinition: Ink, syn. madaAdN , (Msb,) and niqosN , (K,) with which one writes: (S, Msb:) so called because it is one of the means of beautifying writings; (Mohammad Ibn-Zeyd, TA;) or because it beautifies, and makes plain, handwriting; (Hr, TA;) or because of the marks that it leaves: (As, TA:) pl. [of pauc.] A^aHobaArN (IDrst, TA) and [of mult.] HubuwrN . (TA.) ― -b2- I. q. wa$oYN [The variegation, or figuring, of cloth or of a garment; or a kind of variegated, or figured, cloth or garment ]: (IAar, K:) pl. HubuwrN . (K, * TA.) [See also HibarapN .] ― -b3- A mark, or sign, of the enjoyment of ease and plenty: (As, S, K: [in one copy of the S, and in the CK, for A^avaru Aln~aEomapi , I find, erroneously, A^avaru Aln~iEomapi :]) and [hence,] beauty; (As, S, A, K;) beauty of aspect; or a beautiful and pleasing aspect, that satisfies the eye by its comeliness: (As, S, TA:) colour; complexion: (Fr, IAar, S, TA:) pl. A^aHobaArN (S) and HubuwrN . (K, * TA.) One says, A_in~ahu laHasanu AlHibori waAls~ibori Verily he is beautiful, and of goodly appearance: (As, S:) or of beautiful complexion. (IAar.) And *ahaba Hiboruhu wasiboruhu His colour, or complexion, (Fr, S,) or beautiful, (A,) and goodliness of form or aspect, departed: (Fr, S, A:) from the saying, jaA='ati AlA^abilu Hasanapa AlA^aHobaAri waAlA^asobaAri [ The camels came beautiful in colours and in appearances ]. (Fr, S, A. *) One says also, waAls~abori ↓ fulaAnN Hasanu AlHabori : where Hbr seems to be the inf. n. of Habarotuhu “ I made him, or it, beautiful. ” (S.) ― -b4- Also, (S, K,) and ↓ HaborN (TA) and ↓ HabarN (K) and ↓ HabaArN (S, K) and ↓ HibaArN , (A, K,) A mark, or trace, (S, A, K,) of beating, (A,) or of a blow that has not brought blood, or of a healed wound, (TA,) or of work, or labour: (A, TA:) pl. of the first [or second] HubuwrN (Yaakoob, S, K) and [of the first and third, accord. to analogy,] A^aHobaArN ; (TA;) and of the fourth HabaAraAtN , (Yaakoob, S, TA,) it having no broken pl. (TA.) One says, bihi HubuwrN Upon him are marks [of beating, &c.]. (S.) And AlD~arobi ↓ bijilodihi HibaAru Upon his skin is the mark of beating. (A.) And AlEamali ↓ biyadihi HibaAru Upon his hand is the mark of work, or labour. (A.) ― -b5- See also HibirN . ― -b6- And see HubuwrN . -A2- Also, [like the Hebrew ? , and the Chaldee ? ,] A like; an equal; a fellow. (K.) ― -b2- See also HaborN .

sourceDefinition: (S, Mgh, Msb, K) and ↓ HabarapN (K) A [ garment of the kind called ] burod , (S, Mgh,) or a sort of burod , (K,) of the fabric of El-Yemen, (S, Mgh, K,) striped ( munam~arN [or this word, q. v., may perhaps signify spotted ]); (TA;) a kind of garment of the fabric of El-Yemen, of cotton or linen, striped ( muxaT~aTN ): (Msb:) pl. HibarN and HibaraAtN (S, Mgh, Msb, K) and HabarN and HabaraAtN : (TA:) [or rather ↓ HibarN and ↓ HabarN are coll. gen. ns.] Accord. to Lth, (Az, Mgh, TA,) Hbrp is not a place, nor a known thing, but only signifies wa$oYN [see HiborN ]; (Az, Mgh, Msb, TA;) and one says burodN HibarapN (Msb, TA) and buruwdN HibarapN , (TA,) and burodu HibarapK (Mgh, Msb, TA) and buruwdu HibarapK , (Mgh, TA,) like as one says vuwobu qiromizK , the word qrmz signifying a certain dye. (Az, Msb, TA.) [The term ↓ HabarapN is now applied in Egypt to A lady's outer covering of silk, black for the married, and white for the unmarried, worn in ridding and walking abroad; the former worn also by concubine slaves. See also HabiyrN .]

definition: [a word respecting which J says,] its alif [written Y ] is not the fem.
sourceDefinition: [a word respecting which J says,] its alif [written Y ] is not the fem. alif nor the alif of quasi-coordination; [as F says of the alif of qabaEovarFY , though he finds fault with J for saying thus of the alif of HubaAraY ; (see A^alifu Alt~akoviyri , in art. A )] the name [says J] being only composed with it, so that it is as it were a part of the word itself, which is imperfectly decl. when determinate and when indeterminate; i. e., without tenween: (S:) but its alif is the fem. alif; for were it not so, it would be perfectly decl.; (K;) and J says that it is imperfectly decl.: (TA:) and his saying that the alif is [as it were] a part of the word itself is a strange expression, for which it would be difficult to give an answer, and which therefore requires not exorbitance: but “ it is sufficient excellence for a man that his faults may be counted: ” (M:) [ A species of bustard; ] a certain bird, (S, Msb, K,) well known, of the form of the goose, with a dustcolour upon its head and belly, and the back and wings of which are for the most part of the colour of the quail; (Msb;) or it is a long-necked bird, of an ash-colour, of the form of the goose, with a beak somewhat long, and that is preyed upon, but does not itself prey: Az says that it does not drink water, and that it lays its eggs in distant sands: [the truth is, that it drinks seldom: the male bird has a pouch, extending from beneath the tongue to the breast, said to be large enough to contain seven quarts of water; and it has been supposed by some that he fills this with water for the supply of himself and his mate:] and Az further says, We used, when we journeyed, to proceed in the mountains of EdDahnà, and sometimes we picked up in one day between four and eight of its eggs: it lays four eggs, of a bluish colour, more delicious in taste than those of the domestic hen and than those of the ostrich: and others say that it brings its food from a greater distance than any other bird; sometimes from a distance of many days' journey: also, that it is constantly provided with a thin excrement, or dung, which it voids upon the hawk when pursued by the latter; thus saving itself, by preventing the hawk from continuing its flight, and, as some say, causing its feathers to drop off: whence the prov., A^asolaHu mino HubaAraY : [see art. slH :] (TA:) HubaAraY is applied alike to the male and the female, and used as sing. and pl.: (S, K:) but it has pl. forms, (TA,) namely, HubaArayaAtN (S, Msb, K, TA) and HubaAraAtN : (TA:) accord. to Sb, it has not HabaArK , [in the TA incorrectly written HabaAriY , as though it had the article Al prefixed to it, or were prefixed to another noun,] nor HabaAy^iru , [though both of these are mentioned as pls. of it in several of the grammars of the Arabs,] in order to distinguish between HubaAraY and nouns of the measures faEolaA='u and fiEaAlapN and the like. (TA.) It is said in a prov., wakul~u $aYo'K qado yuHib~u waladaho Hat~aY AlHubaAraY wataTiyru Eanadahu [ And everything certainly loves its offspring: even the bustard; and it flies by its side ]: (S, Mgh: *) [in the TA, wayadif~u Eanadaho :] it flies by the side of its young one to teach it to fly before its wings have grown, because of its stupidity: (TA:) the HbArY is thus specially mentioned because it is proverbial for stupidity, and, notwithstanding its stupidity, loves its offspring, and teaches it to fly. (S, Mgh.) Another prov. is, fulaAnN may~ito kamada AlHubaAraY [ Such a one is dying with the concealed grief of the bustard ]: because the HbArY moults with other birds, but its new feathers are slow in coming: so when the other birds fly, it is unable to do so, and dies of concealed grief. (TA.) [See also HuboruwrN , and yaHobuwrN .]

definition: , (S, A, Msb, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, A, Msb, K,) aor. , (S, K,) inf. n. HarodN , (S, Msb,) He tended, repaired, betook himself, or directed himself or his course or aim, to or towards; made for or towards; aimed at; sought, pursued, desired, or intended; (him, or it; IAar, K;) syn. qaSada . (IAar, S, A, Msb, K.) Agreeably with this explanation, some render the words of the Kur [lxviii. 25], wagadawoA EalaY HarodK qaAdiriyna . (S.) You say to a man, ↓ qado Haradotu Harodaka I have tended, repaired, &c., to, or towards, thee; like qaSadotu qaSodaka (Fr, S, * L) and A^aqobalotu qibalaka . (Fr, L.) A rájiz says, (S,) namely, Hassán, (so in a copy of the S,) A^aqobala sayolN jaA='a mino A^amori A@ll~`ha yaHoridu Haroda Aljan~api Almugil~aho [ A torrent advanced, that came by the command of God, tending to the fruitful garden ]. (S.) -A2- Also, aor. , (K,) inf. n. HarodN , (S, L,) He prevented, hindered, impeded, withheld, restrained, debarred, inhibited, forbade, prohibited, or interdicted; (IAar, S, K;) and so ↓ Hr~d , (L, K,) inf. n. taHoriydN . (TA.) Agreeably with this explanation, also, some render the words of the Kur cited above: from HaAradato said of she-camels, meaning “ they became scanty in their supplies of milk. ” (S.) -A3- Also, aor. , (S, L, K,) or , (AZ, S, L,) inf. n. HuruwdN ; (S, K;) [and app. ↓ tHr~d and ↓ AnHrd ; (see HariydN ;)] He (a man) separated himself from others; (K;) he left, or abandoned, or forsook, his people, and removed from them; (AZ, S;) he retired from his people, and alighted, or took up his abode, in a place by himself. (S.) -A4- Harida , (Sb, S, Msb, K,) aor. , (Msb, K,) and Harada , aor. , (L, K,) inf. n. HarodN , (Sb, As, T, IDrd, S, Msb, &c.,) so says Aboo-Nasr Ahmad Ibn-Hátim, companion of As, (S,) and HaradN , (T, S, Msb,) this latter form of the inf. n. sometimes used, accord. to ISk, (S,) and this is the form heard by AZ and AO and As from the Arabs of chaste speech, (TA,) but both forms are chaste, (IAar, TA,) though the former is the more common, (IAar, Msb,) He was, or became, angry: (S, Msb, K, &c.:) he was, or became, exasperated ( tHr~$ ) by one who angered him, and desired to kill him. (T, L.) And Harada Ealayohi (A, L) and Harida (L) He was angry with him. (A, L.) -A5- Harida , (S, Msb, K,) aor. , (S, K,) inf. n. HaradN , (S, Mgh, Msb,) He (a camel) had the disease termed HaradN [q. v.]: (K:) he had the tendons, or sinews, of one of his fore legs relaxed by the cord whereby the fore shank is sometimes bound up to the arm, or had them in that state naturally, (S, Mgh, Msb, *) so that he shook his fore legs, (S,) or so that he beat the ground [ with the fore leg ], (Mgh, Msb,) in walking, or going: (S, Mgh, Msb:) or he (a camel) had the tendon, or sinew, of his arm broken, so that his fore leg became lax, and he never ceased to shake it: the tendon, or sinew, breaks only in the outer side of the arm, and it [the arm] seems, when the camel walks or is in motion, as though it stretched, by reason of his raising it so high from the ground, and by reason of its laxness: (ISh, TA:) or he (a beast) raised his legs very high, in walking, or going, and put them down in their place, by reason of his being very short in his step. (L.) ― -b2- Also, aor. and inf. n. as above, He (a man) was oppressed by the weight of his coat of mail, so that he was unable to stretch himself out in walking. (K.) ― -b3- And, with the same aor. and inf. n., It (a bowstring) had one or more of the several portions of which ( by their being twisted together ) it was composed longer than others. (K.)

(IAar, S, A, Msb, K.) Agreeably with this explanation, some render the words of the Kur [lxviii. 25], wagadawoA EalaY HarodK qaAdiriyna . (S.) You say to a man, ↓ qado Haradotu Harodaka I have tended, repaired, &c., to, or towards, thee; like qaSadotu qaSodaka (Fr, S, * L) and A^aqobalotu qibalaka . (Fr, L.) A rájiz says, (S,) namely, Hassán, (so in a copy of the S,) A^aqobala sayolN jaA='a mino A^amori A@ll~`ha yaHoridu Haroda Aljan~api Almugil~aho [ A torrent advanced, that came by the command of God, tending to the fruitful garden ]. (S.) -A2- Also, aor. , (K,) inf. n. HarodN , (S, L,) He prevented, hindered, impeded, withheld, restrained, debarred, inhibited, forbade, prohibited, or interdicted; (IAar, S, K;) and so ↓ Hr~d , (L, K,) inf. n. taHoriydN . (TA.) Agreeably with this explanation, also, some render the words of the Kur cited above: from HaAradato said of she-camels, meaning “ they became scanty in their supplies of milk. ” (S.) -A3- Also, aor. , (S, L, K,) or , (AZ, S, L,) inf. n. HuruwdN ; (S, K;) [and app. ↓ tHr~d and ↓ AnHrd ; (see HariydN ;)] He (a man) separated himself from others; (K;) he left, or abandoned, or forsook, his people, and removed from them; (AZ, S;) he retired from his people, and alighted, or took up his abode, in a place by himself. (S.) -A4- Harida , (Sb, S, Msb, K,) aor. , (Msb, K,) and Harada , aor. , (L, K,) inf. n. HarodN , (Sb, As, T, IDrd, S, Msb, &c.,) so says Aboo-Nasr Ahmad Ibn-Hátim, companion of As, (S,) and HaradN , (T, S, Msb,) this latter form of the inf. n. sometimes used, accord. to ISk, (S,) and this is the form heard by AZ and AO and As from the Arabs of chaste speech, (TA,) but both forms are chaste, (IAar, TA,) though the former is the more common, (IAar, Msb,) He was, or became, angry: (S, Msb, K, &c.:) he was, or became, exasperated ( tHr~$ ) by one who angered him, and desired to kill him. (T, L.) And Harada Ealayohi (A, L) and Harida (L) He was angry with him. (A, L.) -A5- Harida , (S, Msb, K,) aor. , (S, K,) inf. n. HaradN , (S, Mgh, Msb,) He (a camel) had the disease termed HaradN [q. v.]: (K:) he had the tendons, or sinews, of one of his fore legs relaxed by the cord whereby the fore shank is sometimes bound up to the arm, or had them in that state naturally, (S, Mgh, Msb, *) so that he shook his fore legs, (S,) or so that he beat the ground [ with the fore leg ], (Mgh, Msb,) in walking, or going: (S, Mgh, Msb:) or he (a camel) had the tendon, or sinew, of his arm broken, so that his fore leg became lax, and he never ceased to shake it: the tendon, or sinew, breaks only in the outer side of the arm, and it [the arm] seems, when the camel walks or is in motion, as though it stretched, by reason of his raising it so high from the ground, and by reason of its laxness: (ISh, TA:) or he (a beast) raised his legs very high, in walking, or going, and put them down in their place, by reason of his being very short in his step. (L.) ― -b2- Also, aor. and inf. n. as above, He (a man) was oppressed by the weight of his coat of mail, so that he was unable to stretch himself out in walking. (K.) ― -b3- And, with the same aor. and inf. n., It (a bowstring) had one or more of the several portions of which ( by their being twisted together ) it was composed longer than others. (K.)

definition: A bundle of reeds, or canes, which is laid upon the rafters, or pieces of wood;
sourceDefinition: A bundle of reeds, or canes, which is laid upon the rafters, or pieces of wood; (called rawaAfidu , IAar, L,) of a roof: (IAar, Mgh, Msb:) [the reeds, or canes, which are thus used in the construction of a roof are tied together in small bundles, each of which I have generally found to consist of about five or six: over them is added a coat of plaster:] pl. HaraAdiY~u : a Nabathæan word: (S, Mgh, Msb, K:) arabicized: (S:) you should not say hurodiY~N . (ISk, S, Mgh.) ― -b2- Also, (L, K,) and ↓ Hurodiy~apN , (Mgh, L, K,) The girdle ( HiyaASap , Mgh, L, K, TA, in the CK HiyADap ) of a fold for sheep, &c. ( HaZiyrap ), which is bound upon the fence ( HaAy^iT ) of reeds, or canes, (Mgh, L, K,) crosswise: (Mgh, L:) accord. to IDrd, Nabathæan. (L.) You say, ↓ Har~adahu , inf. n. taHoriydN . (L.) ― -b3- Also ↓ Hurodiy~apN , (Lth, Msb,) in the 'Eyn hurodiy~apN , (Mgh,) but this latter is disallowed by ISk, (Msb,) Reeds, or canes, which are connected, in a bent form, with the arched branches ( TaAqaAt ) of a grape-vine, (Lth, Mgh, Msb,) and upon which the shoots of the vine are let fall. (Mgh.) ― -b4- Also HurodiY~N , with damm, [irregularly formed from HirodN , unless it be a mistake for HirodiY~N ,] A man having wide, or capacious, intestines [like those of the camel]. (L, TA.)

definition: A man who separates himself from others;
sourceDefinition: A man who separates himself from others; as also ↓ HaridN and ↓ HarodN and ↓ HaAridN and ↓ mutaHar~idN (K) and ↓ HarodaAnu : (L:) fem. Hariydapu , not HarodaY : (L:) or a man who has left, or abandoned, or forsaken, his people, and removed from them: (AZ, S:) or a sole, or single, man: (As, S:) and ↓ munoHaridN signifies solitary, in the dial. of Hudheyl: (As, S:) pl. (Er-Rághib, TA.) You say, A^aHosanotu A_ilayohi and bihi [ I acted, or behaved, with goodness, well, or in a good or comely or pleasing manner, towards him; did good to him; benefited him; conferred a benefit, or benefits, upon him ]: both signify the same: (S, TA:) and hence, in the Kur [xii. 101], qado A^aHosana biY A_i*a A^axorajaniY mina Als~ijoni meaning A_ilaY~a [i. e. He hath acted well towards me, when he brought me forth from the prison ]: (AHeyth, Az:) or, accord. to some, the verb in this case is made to import the meaning of laTafa [which is trans. by means of bi , i. e. He hath acted graciously with me ]. (Mughnee in art. bi .) ― -b3- AlA_iHosaAnu is also explained as meaning AlA_ixolaASu [i. e. Aln~aAsu A^abonaA='u maA yuHosinuwna is another saying of 'Alee, meaning (tropical:) Men are named, or reputed, in relation to what they know, and to the good deeds that they do. (TA.) ― -b3- A^aHosino bihi and maA A^aHosanahu : see 1, last sentence. You say also, ↓ maA A^uHayosinahu [i. e. sourceDefinition: (S, K, &c.) and ↓ HusunN , which is of the dial. of El-Hijáz, and ↓ HasanN , (MF, TA,) Goodness, or goodliness, [generally the latter,] beauty, comeliness, or pleasingness; contr. of quboHN : (S:) i. q. jamaAlN : (K:) but accord. to As, [when relating to the person,] HusonN is in the eyes, and jamaAlN is in the nose: (TA:) symmetry; or just proportion of the several parts of the person, one to another: (Kull:) or anything, moving the mind, that is desired, or wished for; such as is approved by the intellect; and such as is approved by natural desire; and such as is approved by the faculty of sense: in the common conventional language, mostly applied to what is approved by the sight: in the Kur, mostly to what is approved by mental perception: it is in accidents as well as in substances: (Er-Rághib, TA:) the pl. is ↓ maHaAsinu , (S, K,) like malaAmiHu pl. of lamoHapN , and ma$aAbihu pl. of $abahN , &c., (Har p. 9,) contr. to rule, (S, K,) as though pl. of ↓ maHosanN or ↓ muHosanN : (S accord. to different copies:) or, accord. to Lh and Eth-Tha'álibee, maHaAsinu has no proper sing. (TA.) wa quwluwA liln~aAsi HusonFA , in the Kur [ii. 77], means And say ye to men a saying having in it goodness ( qawolFA *aA HusonK ): or HusonFA may mean HasanFA : (Zj, TA:) and some read here HasanFA : and some, HusunFA , accord. to the dial. of El-Hijáz: and some, ↓ HusonaY , as an inf. n., like bu$oraY : (Bd:) but AHát and Zj disallow this; the former saying that HusonaY is like fuEolaY [as fem. of A^afoEalu denoting the comparative and superlative degrees], and therefore should have the article Al . (TA.) wa waS~ayonaA AlA_inosaAna biwaAlidayohi HusonFA , in the Kur [xxix. 7], means [in like manner] And we have enjoined man to do to his two parents what is good ( maA yaHosunu HusonFA ): (TA:) and here [also] some read HasanFA ; and some, A_iHosaAnFA . (Bd.) [See another ex. of a similar kind, from the Kur xviii. 85, voce A_im~aA , near the beginning of the paragraph.] ― -b2- sit~u AlHusoni [ The convolvulus caïricus of Linn.; abundant in the gardens of Cairo;] a certain plant that twines about trees and has a beautiful flower. (TA.) ― -b3- See also HasanN .

definition: Having, or possessing, the quality termed HusonN [which see above;
sourceDefinition: Having, or possessing, the quality termed HusonN [which see above; good, or goodly, (generally the latter,) beautiful, comely, pleasing or pleasant, &c.]; (Msb, K, TA;) either intrinsically, as when applied to belief in God and in his attributes; or extrinsically, as when applied to war against unbelievers, for this is not good in itself: said to be the only epithet of its measure except baTalN : (TA:) and ↓ HasiynN signifies the same, (IB, K,) because from Hasuna , like EaZiymN and karyimN from EaZuma and karuma , (IB, TA,) and ↓ HusaAnN , (K,) but this is an intensive epithet, [signifying very good or goodly &c.,] (IB, TA,) and ↓ Hus~aAnN , (K,) also an intensive epithet, (S, IB,) and ↓ HaAsinN , (K,) [properly signifying being, or becoming, good or goodly &c.,] cited by Lh as used in a future sense, (TA,) and ↓ muHas~anN as applied to a face: (K:) the fem. is HasanapN , and ↓ HasonaA='u , applied to a woman, (S, Msb, K,) though the corresponding masc. of this latter, namely, ↓ A^aHosanu , is [said to be] not used (S, K) as applied to a man [in the sense of HasanN ], (S,) [but the phrase huwa A^aHosanuhumo wajohFA as meaning Hasanuhumo wajohFA is mentioned in the S in art. byD , (see bayaADN , and see also the pl. A^aHaAsinu in what here follows,)] and ↓ Hus~aAnapN : (S, K:) the pl. masc. is HisaAnN , (Msb, K,) pl. of HasanN used as an epithet; but when HasanN is used as a [proper] name, its pl. is Hasanuwna ; (Msb;) and HisaAnN may also be pl. of HasiynN ; (TA;) and Hus~aAnuwna , (Sb, K,) pl. of ↓ Hus~aAnN , which has no broken pl.: (Sb:) and A^aHaAsinu Alqawomi means HisaAnuhumo [ the good, or goodly, &c., of the party, or company of men ]: (K:) the pl. fem. is HisaAnN , (K,) like the masc., pl. of HasonaA='u , and the only instance of its kind except EijaAfN , pl. of EajofaA='u . (TA.) You say rajulN HasanN basanN [ A man very good or goodly &c.], using bsn as an imitative sequent [for the purpose of corroboration]. (S.) ― -b2- [ HadiyvN HasanN A tradition of good authority; generally applied to one transmitted in the first instance by two or more relaters. ― -b3- Also meaning Good, comely, goodhumoured, pleasing, or pleasant, discourse or talk. ] ― -b4- AlHasanu The bone that is next to the elbow; as also ↓ AlHusonu : (K:) or the extremity of the bone of the upper half of the arm next the shoulder-joint, because of the abundance of flesh that is upon it; the extremity of that bone next the elbow being called AlqabiyHu : (TA in art. qbH :) or the upper part of that bone; the lower part thereof being called AlqbyH . (Fr, TA in that art.) ― -b5- A kind of tree, of beautiful appearance, (K, TA,) also called the A^alA=' , that grows in rows upon a hill, or heap, ( kaviyb ,) of sand; so called because of its beauty; whence the kvyb is called naqaA AlHasani : thus described by Az, on the authority of 'Alee Ibn-Hamzeh. (TA.) ― -b6- [And hence, perhaps,] HasanN signifies also A high kaviyb [or hill, or heap, of sand ]: (IAar, K:) whence it is used as a [proper] name of a boy. (IAar, TA.) -A2- See also HusonN , first sentence.

sourceDefinition: , fem. HasonaA='u , pl. A^aHaAsinu : see HasanN . ― -b2- AlA^aHosanu denotes the comparative and superlative degrees [of HusonN ]; as in the phrase huwa AlA^aHosanu [ He, or it, is the better, and best; or the more, and most, goodly or beautiful or comely &c.]: (K:) ↓ AlHusonaY is the fem.; as in the phrase AlA^asomaA='u AlHusonaY The best names; those of God; which are ninety and nine: (Jel in vii. 179:) it signifies the contr. of Als~uwo'aY : (S, K:) the pl. of AlA^aHosanu is AlA^aHaAsinu . (K.) In the saying, in the Kur [vi. 153 and xvii. 36], wa laA taqorabuwA maAla Alyatiymi A_il~aA biAl~atiY hiYa A^aHosanu [ And approach ye not the property of the orphan, to make use of it,] except by that act which is best to be done with it, the meaning is, such an act as the taking care of it, and increasing it: (Bd:) or, as some say, the meaning is, the taking, of his property, what will [suffice to] conceal those parts of one's person that should not be exposed, and stay one's hunger. It means also, [as an epithet in which the quality of a subst. predominates, That which is better, and that which is best. And hence,] The good final or ultimate state or condition [appointed for the faithful]: (K:) so, it is said, in the Kur xli. 50. (TA.) The pl. of ↓ AlHusonaY is AlHusonayaAtu and ↓ AlHusanu , (K, [the latter like rujaEN pl. of rujoEaY , but misunderstood by Freytag as syn. with AlmaHaAsinu , which next follows it in the K,]) neither of which is used without the article Al . (TA.)

definition: Confined, kept in, prevented from escape, retained, restrained, or withheld;
sourceDefinition: Confined, kept in, prevented from escape, retained, restrained, or withheld; as also ↓ maHoquwnN . (K.) ― -b2- And, as a subst., (S,) Milk collected in a skin, (S, IF, Msb,) when fresh milk has been poured upon that which has become curdled, or thick, or upon that which has been churned. (S, TA.) Hence the prov., A^abaY AlHaqiynu AlEi*orapa ; i. e. AlEu*ora ; [ The milk collected in the skin, &c., has disallowed the excuse; ] (A 'Obeyd, S, TA;) applied to him who excuses himself when having no [real] excuse: (TA:) originally said by a man who asked some people to give him milk to drink, upon their excusing themselves while they had milk which they had collected in a skin; meaning, this Hqbn belies you. (A 'Obeyd, TA.)

definition: A man keeping in, or retaining, and collecting, his urine;
sourceDefinition: A man keeping in, or retaining, and collecting, his urine; from HaqiynN meaning “ milk collected in a skin: ” (IF, Msb:) [ suffering from retention of the urine: ] having urine that distresses [ by its quantity ]: (S, TA:) having much urine retained and collected: (Mgh:) and ↓ HaqinN signifies the same. (TA.) Hence the saying, (Mgh, TA,) in a trad., (TA,) laA raA^oYa liHaAqinK walaA HaAqibK walaA HaAziqK (S, * Mgh, TA *) No counsel, or advice, is possible to one who has much urine retained and collected, nor to one suffering suppression of the feces, nor to one who is pinched by a tight boot. (Mgh, TA. *) ― -b2- [ Collecting grease, or melted grease, in a skin. ] You say, A^anaA minohu kaHaAqini AlA_ihaAlapi (assumed tropical:) I am a person skilled in it; because such a one does not collect the AhAlp in a skin until he knows that it has cooled, lest the skin should be burnt. (K.) ― -b3- (assumed tropical:) A moon a little after or before the change ( hilaAl ) having its two extremities elevated, and its back decumbent. (K.) Hence the saying, hilaAlN waAqifN xayorN mino hilaAlK HaAqinK (tropical:) [ A hlAl erect (here meaning nearly erect ) is better, or more auspicious, than a hlAl decumbent ]. (A, TA.) [See also A^a*ofaqu .]

definition: The stomach; (K;) an epithet in which the quality of a subst. is predominant; because it retains, or collects, the food: (TA:) and the pit between each collar-bone and what is termed Habolu AlEaAtiqi...
sourceDefinition: The stomach; (K;) an epithet in which the quality of a subst. is predominant; because it retains, or collects, the food: (TA:) and the pit between each collar-bone and what is termed Habolu AlEaAtiqi [explained in art. Hbl , q. v.]; (AA, S, K; *) the two together being termed [the] HaAqinataAni : (AA, S:) the pit of each collar-bone: (T, TA:) the part between the collar-bone and the neck: (TA:) or the lower part of the belly: (S, K:) pl. AlHawaAqinu . (T, TA.) [See also Al*~aAqinapu .] Hence, (K,) it is said in a prov., laA^uloHiqan~a HawaAqinaka bi*awaAqiniki , (S, K,) i. e. [ I will assuredly conjoin ] the lower part of thy belly with the upper part thereof: or the part of thy belly that retains, or collects, the food, with the lower part of thy belly, and with thy knees. (TA.) The *aAqinap is [also said to be] the extremity of the Huloquwm [or windpipe]: and hence the saying attributed to 'Áïsheh, that the Prophet died [with his head] between her HaAqinap and her *aAqinap . (S.)

definition: Hard, firm, strong, strict, or rigorous, in religion, and in fight, (S, K,) and in courage;
sourceDefinition: Hard, firm, strong, strict, or rigorous, in religion, and in fight, (S, K,) and in courage; (TA;) as also ↓ HamisN : (S, K:) pl. of the former, HumosN . (K.) ― -b2- Hence, A pious man, who carefully abstains from unlawful things: because he exceeds the usual bounds in matters of religion, and is hard to himself; as also ↓ mutaHam~isN . (TA.) ― -b3- Sing. of AlHumosu , (Mgh,) which latter is an epithet applied to The tribes of Kureysh (S, A, K) and Kináneh (S, K) and Jedeeleh, (K,) i. e. Jedeeleh of Keys, consisting of [ the tribes of ] Fahm and and 'Adwán the two sons of 'Amr the son of Keys the son of 'Eylán, and the Benoo- 'Ámir Ibn- Saasa'ah, (AHeyth, TA,) and their followers in the Time of Ignorance; (K;) or to Kureysh and their coreligionists; (Mgh;) because of the hardships which they imposed upon themselves in matters of religion, (S, A, Mgh, K,) as well as in courage, (TA,) for they used not to enjoy the shade in the days of Minè, nor to enter the houses by their doors, (S, Mgh, TA,) while they were in the state of A_iHoraAm , (TA,) nor to clarify butter, nor to pick up [dung such as is called] jal~ap , (S, L,) or baEor , (TA,) [for fuel,] and they dwelt in the Haram, (AHeyth, TA,) and did not go forth in the days of the mawosim to 'Arafát, but halted at El-Muzdelifeh, (AHeyth, Mgh, TA,) saying, “ We are the people of God, and we go not forth from the Haram: ” (AHeyth, TA:) or they were thus called because they made their abode in the Haram: (Sgh, TA:) or because they betook themselves for refuge to the HamosaA=' ( AlHamosaA='u ), which is the Kaabeh, so called because its stones are white inclining to blackness: (K:) the Benoo- 'Ámir were of the Humos , though not of the inhabitants of the Haram, because their mother was of the tribe of Kureysh: the term AlA^aHomaAsu also, [pl. of ↓ HamisN or of ↓ HamiysN ,] is applied to those of the Arabs whose mothers were of the tribe of Kureysh. (TA.) ― -b4- Also Courageous; (Sb, S, K;) and so ↓ HamiysN and ↓ HamisN : (K:) pl. [of the first, masc. only,] A^aHaAmisu and [masc. and fem.] HumosN and [of the second or third] A^aHomaAsN . (TA.) AlA^aHaAmisu is also said to be applied to The tribe of Kureysh: or, accord. to some, to the Benoo- 'Ámir, because descendants of Kureysh: the former is said by IAar. (TA.) ― -b5- Hence, (A, TA,) waqaEa fiY hinodi AlA^aHaAmisi , (A, TS, K,) or laqiYa hinoda AlA^aHaAmisi , (L,) (tropical:) He fell into distress (A, L) and trial: (A:) or into calamity: (K:) or he died: (K:) or the latter phrase has this last meaning. (ISd, A, and TA in art. hnd .) hinodN was the name of a courageous people of the Arabs. (A, TA.) ― -b6- EaAmN A^aHomasu , (S, A, K,) and sanapN HamosaA='u , (K,) (tropical:) A severe year. (S, A, K.) They say also sinuwna A^aHaAmisu (tropical:) Severe years: (K:) the masc. form [of the epithet] being used because by snwn is meant A^aEowaAmN ; or the epithet being used after the manner of a subst.: (ISd, TA:) and sinuwna HumosN signifies the same: (K:) or the latter, years of hunger. (Az, TA.) ― -b7- najodapN HamosaA='u (assumed tropical:) Vehement [ courage, or fight, &c.]. (TA.) ― -b8- makaAnN A^aHomasu (tropical:) A hard place: (S, K:) or a rugged and hard place: (A:) pl. A^amokinapN HumosN . (K.) You say also A^aroDN A^aHaAmisu , with the pl., meaning, (tropical:) A sterile, barren, or unfruitful, and narrow, land: (A:) or a land in which is no herbage nor pasturage nor rain nor anything. (TA.) And A^araDuwna A^aHaAmisu (tropical:) Sterile, barren, or unfruitful, lands. (S, L.)

sourceDefinition: [The colocynth; cucumis colocynthis; ] a certain bitter plant; (Msb;) [and its fruit; ] well known; (K;) i. q. $aroYN : (S:) n. un. with p : (S, Msb, K: *) [accord. to Freytag (who refers to Avic. p. 175, and Sprengel. hist. rei herb. vol. i. p. 269,) applied also to the momordica elaterium, or cucumis prophetarum: ] there is a male species, and a female; the former fibrous; the latter soft, or easily broken, white, and easy to swallow: (TA:) the choice sort of it is the yellow; (K;) or, accord. to the “ Kánoon ” of the Ra-ees [Ibn-Seenà, from which the description of its properties and uses, in the K and TA, is, with some slight variations, taken], the white, very white, and soft; for the black and the hard are bad, and it is not plucked until it becomes yellow, and the greenness has completely gone from it; (TA:) its pulp attenuates the thick phlegmatic humour that flows upon the joints (K, TA) and tendons, (TA,) when swallowed (K, TA) in the dose of of twelve keeráts, (TA,) or used in the manner of a cluster: it is beneficial for melancholy, and epilepsy, and the [ sort of doting termed ] wasowaAs , and alopecia ( daA=' Alv~aEolab ), and elephantiasis ( Alju*aAm ), (K, TA,) and [ the disease of the tumid leg, termed ] daA=' Alfiyl ; for these three used by rubbing; and for the cold niqoris [i. e. arthritis, or gout ], (TA,) and for the bite of vipers, and the sting of scorpions, especially its root; (K, TA;) for this last being the most beneficial of medicines; a drachm of its root, administered to an Arab stung by a scorpion in four places, being said to have cured him on the spot: that which is plucked green relaxes [ the bowels ] excessively, and produces excessive vomiting: so in the “ Kánoon: ” (TA:) it is also beneficial for the tooth-ache, by fumigating with its seeds; and for killing fleas, by sprinkling what is cooked thereof; and for the sciatica, by rubbing with what is green thereof: (K, TA:) its root is cooked with vinegar, and one rinses the mouth with it for the tooth-ache; and the vinegar is cooked in it in hot ashes: when cooked in olive-oil, that oil, being dropped [ into the ear-hole ], is beneficial for ringing in the ears: it is beneficial also for the moist and flatulent colic: and sometimes it attenuates the blood: administered as a suppository in the vagina, it kills the fœtus: (TA:) when the plant bears a single fruit, this is very deadly. (K, TA.) [See also habiydN .] Accord. to [many of] the leading authorities among the Arabs, (TA,) the n in this word is augmentative; (Msb, TA;) because of their saying, HaZila AlbaEiyru , meaning “ the camel became sick from eating HanoZal ; ” and J and Sgh [and Fei and others] have mentioned it in art. HZl : but ISd says that this is not an evidence of its being radically triliteral; and that HaZila is like DagobapN (as an epithet applied to a woman) from AlD~agaAbiysu , which must be acknowledged to be radically quadriliteral. (TA.)

definition: Of the colour termed Huw~apN [q.
sourceDefinition: Of the colour termed Huw~apN [q. v. suprà]: and also black: (K:) or black by reason of [ intense ] xuDorap [by which may be here meant either greenness, or dark, or ashy, dust-colour ]: (TA:) applied to a horse, i. q. kumayotN [i. e. bay ] overspread with blackness; (TA;) or red in the back; (En-Nadr, TA;) or more yellow than, but nearly the same as, such as is termed A^aHam~u , so that one swears, of such a horse, that he is A^aHam~ : (AO, TA: [see muHolifN :]) applied to a camel, whose xuDorap [here meaning dark, or ashy, dust-colour ] is intermixed with blackness and yellowness: (S:) applied to a man, having [ a brownish colour such as is termed ] sumorapN in the lip; (S;) or having a blackness in the lips, which is approved; (Ham p. 386;) fem. Haw~aA='u , applied to a woman, (S,) and also to a lip ( $afapN ) as meaning red inclining to blackness: (K:) applied to a plant, inclining to blackness by reason of its intense greenness; (K;) and such is the softest of plants: (TA:) the pl. is Huw~N ; occurring in a trad., in which the best of horses are said to be those thus termed: (TA:) the dim. of A^aHowaY is ↓ A^uHayowK , in the dial. of him who says A^usayowidu [instead of A^usay~idu , dim. of A^asowadu ]; but there is a difference of opinion as to the form with idghám: 'Eesà Ibn-'Omar says ↓ A^uHaY~N , making it perfectly decl., which Sb pronounces a mistake: 'Amr Ibn-El-'Alà, or Aboo-'Amr Ibn-El-'Alà, (accord. to different copies of the S,) says ↓ A^uHaY~K , after the manner of A^uHayowK , which, also, Sb disallows: Yoo says ↓ A^uHaY~u , and this, says Sb, is the regular and right form. (S.) [Hence,] bakorapN Haw~aA='N A sheave of a pulley formed of black wood. (TA.) And namolN Huw~N Red ants; called namolu sulayomaAna . (TA.) fajaEalahu guvaA='F A^aHowaY , in the Kur [lxxxvii. 5], means, accord. to Fr, And hath made it (the herbage mentioned before) dried up, black by reason of oldness: or it may mean and hath made it to become gvA=' [or decayed, or dried-up, leaves and stalks, ] after it has been green. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , inf. n. taHiy~apN , (Mgh, Msb, K,) in its primary sense, i. q. ↓ AHyAhu . (Mgh.) You say, Hay~aAka A@ll~`hu , (S, K,) meaning May God preserve thee alive; prolong thy life; or make thee to continue in life; syn. A^aboqaAka ; (Fr, Selemeh Ibn- 'Ásim, K;) as also ↓ AHyAk ; (Selemeh Ibn-'Ásim, TA;) or Eam~araka : (Aboo-'Othmán El-Mázinee, Mgh, TA:) or may God save thee; or make thee to be free from evil, or harm, or the like: (Fr, TA:) or may God make thee to have dominion: (Fr, S, K:) or may God honour thee, and benefit thee. (Ham. p. 489.) And Hay~aAka A@ll~`hu wabay~aAka [explained in art. bY ]. (TA.) And Hay~aA A@ll~`hu wajohaka [ May God preserve thy face: see muHay~FA ]. (Ham p. 23.) ― -b2- Also He said to him Hay~aAka A@ll~`hu , explained above: (Mgh:) originally, he prayed for his life: and then, he prayed for him, absolutely: (Msb:) he saluted him; (K, TA;) and so Hy~Ahu taHiy~apa Almuw^omini : (Lh, TA:) as used in the language of the law, he said to him, salaAmN Ealayoka . (Msb.) ― -b3- [See also taHiy~apN , below.] -A2- Hy~A Alxamosiyna [in the CK (erroneously) Alxamosiyna ↓ HaY~a ] He approached [ the age of ] fifty. (IAar, K, TA.) -A3- Hay~ayatu HaA='F HasanpF and HasanFA [ I wrote a beautiful H ]. (TA in bAb AlAlf All~ynp .)

sourceDefinition: , (inf. n. muHaAyaApN , TA,) i. q. ↓ A^aHoyayotuhaA [i. e. (assumed tropical:) I gave life to, enlivened, or revived, the fire ] by blowing. (K.) (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , (S, Msb, K, &c.,) inf. n. A_iHoyaA='N , (TA,) said of God, (S, Msb,) He made him alive, to live, or be a living being; quickened, endued with life, vivified, [ revivified, revived, or resuscitated, ] him. (S, * Msb, * K.) Hence, in the Kur [lxxv. last verse], A^alayosa *`lika biqaAdirK A^ano yuHoyiYa AlmawotaY , (S, TA,) i. e. Is not That Doer of these things (Jel) [ able to quicken the dead? ]. ― -b2- See also 2, in two places. ― -b3- (assumed tropical:) He (God) endued him with the intellectual faculty: as in the saying, in the Kur [vi. 122], A^awamano kaAna may~itFA faA^aHoyayonaAhu (assumed tropical:) [ And is he who was intellectually dead and whom we have endued with the intellectual faculty...? ]. (Er-Rághib.) ― -b4- See also 3. ― -b5- AHyA AlA^aroDa (assumed tropical:) He (God) revived the earth, or land, by the rain, so as to produce in it plants, or herbage. (TA.) And A^uHoyiyati AlA^aroDu (assumed tropical:) The land was tilled, and made productive. (AHn.) And AHyA AlmawaAti (tropical:) He turned to use the unowned and unused and uncultivated land by walling it round or sowing it or building upon it and the like. (TA.) ― -b6- Also (assumed tropical:) He (a man) found the land to be fruitful, or abundant in herbage, (S, K,) with fresh herbage. (K.) ― -b7- AHyA All~ayola (assumed tropical:) He passed the night in religious service, worship, adoration, or devotion, abstaining from sleep: (TA:) or [simply] he remained awake during the night. (W p. 9.) And AHyA layolatahu He passed his night awake. (MA.) -A2- AHyt Aln~aAqapu The she-camel had living offspring; (S, K;) her offspring seldom, or never, died. (S.) ― -b2- AHyA Alqawomu The people, or company of men, had their cattle living: (K:) or had their cattle in good condition: (AA, S, K:) or had rain, so that their beasts obtained herbage to such a degree that they became fat: (AZ:) or they (themselves) became in a state of abundance of herbage, or plenty. (S, K. [See also 1.])
