sourceDefinition: Bees: pl. of naAy^ibN : (S, K:) from nawobapN “ a turn that falls to a man at a certain time, ” accord. to As: or so called because they feed and return to their place: (S:) and if so, the sing. is nAy^b : (TA:) or so called because they are of a colour inclining to black; (S, from A'Obeyd; or, as in some copies of the S, A'Obeydeh;) or as likened to the nation of negroes called Aln~uwbapu : and if so, the word has no sing. definition: A turn which comes to one, or which one takes;
sourceDefinition: A turn which comes to one, or which one takes; the time at which, or during which, anything is, or is to be, done, or had, in succession; an opportunity: (S, * K, MF:) pl. nuwabN , (S,) which is extr. [with respect to analogy.] (TA.) See nawobN . ― -b2- nawobapN and ↓ niyaAbapN A coming to water, &c., one time, or turn, after a former time, or turn. (S, K.) ― -b3- nawobapN An assembly, a company, troop, or congregated body, of men. (K.)

definition: Abundant good, (K,) that comes again and again [ by turns ].
sourceDefinition: Abundant good, (K,) that comes again and again [ by turns ]. (A.) ― -b2- Hum~aY naAy^ibapN A quotidian fever. (S.) ― -b3- naAy^ibapN Guests coming time after time. (TA, from a trad.) ― -b4- See nuwbN . ― -b5- naAy^ibN One who supplies the place of another; who acts in his place or stead, or as his substitute, lieutenant, deputy, factor, or agent: pl. nuw~aAbN . (Msb.) ― -b6- naAy^ibapN What befalls, betides, or happens, that is afflictive, distressing, difficult, or unfortunate: pl. nawaAy^ibu and nuwabN ; the latter of which is extr.: (TA:) or rather this latter is pl. of nuwbapN , which is syn. with nAy^bp , (MF,) a subst. from naAbahu A^amorN , (S,) [and therefore signifying an accident, or a casualty, &c.; and as such this pl. is not extr., but analogous:] an evil accident; a misfortune; a disaster; a calamity; an affliction: pl. nawaAy^ibu : (S:) only signifying what is evil: (Msb:) or, accord. to some, an accident, whether good or evil: ex. Lebeed says, nawaAy^ibu mino xayorK wa$ar~K kilaAhumaA falaA Alxayoru mamoduwdN walaA Al$~ar~u laAzibu [ Accidents of a good nature, and of an evil, both of them; and neither is the good prolonged, nor the evil constant ]: or what befalls, betides, or happens, to a man, of difficult, arduous, distressing, or afflictive, events, or affairs, and accidents: [ a difficulty, or difficult affair ] in a trad. respecting Kheyber it is said, qasamahaA nuSofayoni nuSofFA linawaAy^ibihi waHaAjaAtihi wanuSofFA bayona Almusolimiyna [ He divided it into two halves; half for his own difficulties, or difficult affairs, and wants, and half among the Muslims ]. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , (S, A, Msb, K,) aor. yahir~u , (S, Msb, K,) inf. n. hariyrN , (S, A, &c.,) said of a dog, [ He snarled, or howled, or whined; ] he uttered a cry less vehement than barking (S, A, Msb, K.) by reason of his little patience of cold; (S, K) A_ilayohi at him. (K.) or barked and grinned, displaying his fangs. (L, TA.) It is said in a trad, A_in~a Alkaloba yahir~u mino waraA='i A^aholihi Verily the dog [ snarls, or] harks and grins, displaying his fangs, behind his master: meaning, that courage is a quality implanted by nature in a man, so that he engages in wars naturally, and from care to defend what should be inviolable, not reckoning upon a reward, like as the dog naturally barks and grins, displaying his tangs, to defend his masters. (L, TA.) ― -b2- hariyrN is also applied to other sounds than the cry of the dog; as in the instance of hariyru Alr~HaY (assumed tropical:) The sound of the turning of the mill-stone. (TA.) You say also har~ati Alqawosu (assumed tropical:) The bow made a sound. (AHn, K.) And the looking of courageous men, one at another, is likened to hariyr . (ISd, Msb.) ― -b3- har~a fiY wajohi Als~aAy^ili (tropical:) He grinned in the face of the beggar, showing his teeth, and looking sternly, austerely, or morosely (A, TA.) ― -b4- [Hence, perhaps,] har~ahu . (S, K,) aor. yahur~u and yahir~a , (K,) [the latter irreg., like yarim~u as aor. of the trans. v. ram~a ,] inf. n. har~N (S, K) and hariyrN . (K,) (tropical:) He disliked, disapproved of or hated, him or it. (S, K.) You say, har~ahu Aln~aAsu (tropical:) The people disliked, &c., his vicinity. (A.) And har~a AlkaAsa . and AlHaroba , (S, A,) inf. n. hariyrN . (S.) (tropical:) He disliked. &c., the cup of wine, and war. (S, A.) -A2- har~ahu Albaroda , (K,) aor. yahur~uhu , inf. n. har~N , (TA,) The cold made him (a dog) [ to snarl, or hand, or whine; or] to cry [ in the manner described above ]; as also ↓ A^ahar~ahu , (K,) inf. n. A_ihoraArN . (TA.) It is said in a proverb, (TA,) *aA naAbK ↓ $ar~N A^ahr~a [ It is, or was, an evil thing that made the fanged animal to snarl, &c.]: alluding to the appearance of the signs and symptoms of evil: the sayer thereof, hearing the cry ( hariyr ) of a dog, feared the assault of evil, and therefore said this to denote the magnitude of the case in his mind: meaning, nought but an evil thing made the fanged animal to cry: and for this reason, the use of an indeterminate word as an inchoative is well. (K.)

sourceDefinition: A male cat; syn. sin~aworN ; (S, A, K:) which latter is uncommon in the language of the Arabs (IAmb, in Msb, art. snr ;) fem. hir~apN : (S, A. Msb, K:) or hir~N is applied to the male and the female; and the latter is sometimes called hrapN (IAmb, Msb:) the pl. of hr~N is hirrpN : and that of hir~apN is hirarN : and the dim. of hir~apN is hurayorapN . (Msb)) -A2- Also, a subst. from har~ahu meaning "he disapproved of, or hated, him or it. " (S) It is said in a proverb, (S,) yaEorifu hir~FA mino br~K (S, A, K,) meaning He knows not him who dislikes or hates him from him who behaves towards him with goodness and affection and gentleness, and regard for his circumstances. (S, TA.) this is the best explanation of it: (TA:) or the action of him who grins in his face, showing his teeth, and looking steraly, austerely, or morosely, from the action of him who holds loving communion with him. (A:) or the calling of sheep or goats, (S,) or the calling of them to water. (K.) from the driving of them: (S:) or the calling of sheep or goats to provender from the calling of them to water: (IAar) or the driving of sheep or goats (Yoo, K) from the calling of them. (Yoo, TA.) It has been explained [more fully] in art. br . (K.)

definition: , (S, A, K,) and haSara bihi , (S, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, A, K,) and haSara bihi , (S, K,) aor. , (K,) inf. n. haSorN , (A, K,) He pulled it: and he inclined it: or he pulled and inclined it: (A, K, TA [but in the last of these, only haSarahu is given in this sense, agreeably with the A:]) he brought it near; (K;) which is near in meaning to “ he inclined it: ” (TA:) he took hold of its (a branch's) head and inclined it towards him: (S:) or he inclined it (a branch) towards him: (A:) or he bent it (a branch) and drew it towards him: (Mgh:) he bent it; namely, a pliant thing, such as a branch and the like: (A, K:) and he broke it without separating: (K:) or he bent it, namely, anything: (A, * K:) as also ↓ AhtSrhu . (K.) Imra-el-Keys says, (S, TA,) using the verb tropically, (TA,) falam~aA tanaAzaEonaA AlHadiyva waA^asomaHato haSarotu biguSonK *iY $amaAriyxa may~aAli And when we discoursed together, and she became compliant, I pulled, (TA,) or, laying hold of its head, inclined towards me, (S,) a branch with fruit-stalks, waving from side to side: the poet meaning, by the branch, her body, because bending, and soft or supple, like a branch, and likening her hair to the fruit-stalks of the raceme of a palm-tree, in respect of its abundance and luxuriance. (TA.) And it is said in a trad., respecting the building of the mosque of Kubà, rafaEa HajarFA vaqiylFA fahaSarahu A_ilaY baTonihi He raised a heavy stone, and inclined it towards his belly. (TA.) And in another trad., kaAna A_i*aA rakaEa haSara Zahorahu He used, when he bowed himself [ in prayer ], to bend down his back towards the ground: (TA:) or haSara Zahorahu signifies he bent his back much, making it even with his neck. (Mgh.) ― -b2- (tropical:) He pushed him or it; so accord. to all the copies of the K; but accord. to other authorities, (tropical:) he pressed or squeezed, him or it: and he pressed, or squeezed, him or it vehemently. (TA.) You say, haSara qironahu , aor. and inf. n. as above, (tropical:) He pressed, or squeezed, his adversary. (TA.) ― -b3- Also, (K,) or haSarahu [alone], (S,) (assumed tropical:) He broke it; (S, K;) as also ↓ AhtSrhu . (S.) You say of a lion, haSara Alfariysapa , (A, TA,) aor. and inf. n. as above, (tropical:) He broke [ the neck of ] the prey, and inclined it towards him. (TA.) And haSara raA^osa Alfariysapi , and biraA^osihaA , (A, TA,) (tropical:) He [ broke the head of, or] slew the prey. (TA.) -A2- haSira jad~uhu , aor. , [inf. n. haSarN ,] (tropical:) His good fortune declined. (TA.)

Imra-el-Keys says, (S, TA,) using the verb tropically, (TA,) falam~aA tanaAzaEonaA AlHadiyva waA^asomaHato haSarotu biguSonK *iY $amaAriyxa may~aAli And when we discoursed together, and she became compliant, I pulled, (TA,) or, laying hold of its head, inclined towards me, (S,) a branch with fruit-stalks, waving from side to side: the poet meaning, by the branch, her body, because bending, and soft or supple, like a branch, and likening her hair to the fruit-stalks of the raceme of a palm-tree, in respect of its abundance and luxuriance. (TA.) And it is said in a trad., respecting the building of the mosque of Kubà, rafaEa HajarFA vaqiylFA fahaSarahu A_ilaY baTonihi He raised a heavy stone, and inclined it towards his belly. (TA.) sourceDefinition: , aor. yavibu , inf. n. wavobN and wuvuwbN (the latter agreeable with analogy, TA,) and wavabaAnN and waviybN (S, K) and wivAabN (K; but this is generally affirmed to be an inf. n. of waAvaba , TA;) and vibapN , (Ibn-Málik and others) He leaped; jumped; sprang; bounded: (S, K:) or he leaped down, or downwards. (Mgh, Msb, art. Tfr .) ― -b2- wavaba AlmawoDiEa [ He leaped, or jumped, upon, or over the place ]. (TA.) ― -b3- wavaba A_ilaY Al$~arafi wavobapF (tropical:) [ He made a single leap to eminence, or nobility ]. (TA.) ― -b4- wavaba A_ilayohi [app., He leaped, or sprang up, or he hastened, to him ]. (TA.) ― -b5- Alwuvuwbu , except in the dial. of Himyer, signifies The act of rising, or standing up. (TA.) ― -b6- It is also much used by the vulgar as signifying The act of hastening to a thing; as observed by MF, who is wrong in saying that there is nothing in the lexicons that favours its being so used. (TA.) -A2- wavaba , [aor. yavibu ,] inf. n. wavobN , in the dial. of Himyer signifies He sat; sat down. (K, TA, from a trad.) vibo in that dial. signifies Sit; sit down. (S.) It is related that Zeyd Ibn-Abd-Allah Ibn-Dárim came as an envoy to one of the kings of Himyer, and found him at a hunting-place belonging to him, on a high mountain, and he saluted him, and mentioned to him his lineage, or relationship; whereupon the king said to him vibo , meaning A_ijoliso , Sit; but the man thought that he commanded him to leap from the mountain; and he said, “ Thou shalt find me, O king, very obedient: ” then he leaped from the mountain, and perished. So the king said, “ What ailed him? ” And they explained to him his case, and his mistake respecting the word: upon which he said layosato EinodanaA Earabiy~ato mano daxala ZafaAri Ham~ara i. e., [“ Arabic is not current with us: ” (for, probably, in the time of this king, the term Earabiy~ap was only applied to the general language of Arabia:) “ whoso entereth Dhafári,] let him learn [or, rather, speak, as MF says,] the Himyeree language. ” (Mz., 16th nwE .) [The principal facts of this anecdote are also mentioned in the S, on the authority of As.] By the king's saying Earabiy~ato was meant AlEarabiy~apu : the p is pronounced t in the case of a pause (which is the case here) in their dialect. (S.) Or, accord. to another relation of the above anecdote, the king said layosa EinodanaA Earabiy~ato kaEarabiy~atokumo [“ Arabic like your Arabic is not current with us: ”] and this, says ISd, is the right reading in my opinion: for the king did not mean to exclude himself from the Arabs. (MF.)

definition: A certain plant, (S, A, Msb, K,) of a yellow colour, (S, Msb,) resembling sesame, (A, K,) with which one dyes, (A, Msb,) and of which is made the [ liniment called ] gumorap for the face, (S,)...
sourceDefinition: A certain plant, (S, A, Msb, K,) of a yellow colour, (S, Msb,) resembling sesame, (A, K,) with which one dyes, (A, Msb,) and of which is made the [ liniment called ] gumorap for the face, (S,) existing in El-Yemen, (S, K,) and nowhere else, (K,) being there sown; (Msb;) it is not wild, but is sown one year, and remains ten years, (AHn, M,) or twenty years, (K,) without ceasing to be profitable, resembling sesame in its manner of growth; and when it dries, on its attaining to maturity, its pericarps ( xaraAy^iT ) burst, and it is shaken, and the waros shakes out from it: (AHn, M,) it is useful for the [ discolouration of the face termed ] kalaf , used as a liniment; and for the [ leprous-like discolouration of the skin termed bahaq , [ prepared ] as a drink; and the wearing of a garment dyed with it strengthens the venereal faculty: (K:) or a certain yellow dye: or, as some say, a certain plant, of sweet odour: or, as is said in the qaAnuwn [of Ibn-Seenà, or Avicenna,] a certain thing of an intensely red colour, resembling powdered saffron, brought from El-Yemen, and said to be scraped or rubbed off, or to fall off, from its trees: (Mgh:) or, as some say, a species of kurokum , q. v.: or, as some say, resembling kurokum : (Msb:) or a certain thing, yellow, like the [ garments of the kind called mulaA=' , that comes forth upon the [ trees called ] rimov , between the last part of summer and the first part of winter, (M, TA,) which, when it touches a garment, soils it: (TA:) or it also, sometimes, [accord. to certain persons who seems to misapply the word, is a substance which ] pertains to the [ trees called ] EaroEar and rimov , and to other trees, above all in Abyssinia; but this is inferior to that first mentioned (K, TA) in virtue and properties: as to that of the ErEr , it is found between its rind and the main substance, when it dries up; and when it is rubbed, it rubs off; and there is no good in it; but wrs [properly so called] is adulterated with it: and as to that of the rmv , when it is the end of summer, and it has attained its utmost state, it becomes intensely yellow, so that what envelops it becomes yellow, and with this also one adulterates: so says AHn: (TA:) wrs is called in Persian AsPrk [ A_isoPariko ]; and in Turkish, A=lAjhrh . (TK.) [Freytag adds to what he has given on this word from the K, S, TK. as follows: “ Memecylon tinctorium. Sprengel. hist. med., t. ii., p. 444, ed. tert. (ubi wrz scriptum est). Spreng. hist. rei herb., t. i., p. 258. Avicenn. p. 165 ”]

sourceDefinition: a word used to. denote compassion, or pity, and admiration of one's beauty; (M, K;) the object being a child; (K;) as when one says of a child, wayosahu maA A^amolaHahu [ Merry on him! or the like: how beautiful is he! ]: (TA:) or wayosN and wayoHN are used in the place of wayolN ; (TA;) and wayosN lahu signifies wayolN lahu [ Woe to him! ]: (M, TA:) or, as some say, wayosN is a word denoting contempt; and has no verb; analogy forbidding that it should have one: (IJ, M:) Aboo-Turáb says, I heard Abu-sSemeyda' say, wayosN and wayoHN and wayolN have one meaning: (TA:) or wayosaka is not said except to children; and wayolaka is an expression in which is roughness and reproach; and wyH is a gentle and good expression. (AHát, TA.) See wyoHN and wayolN and wayobN . ― -b2- It also signifies Poverty. (ISk, M.) And one may say, if it be right to say so to one, wayosN lahu as meaning Poverty be to him. (ISk.) ― -b3- Also, What a man desires. (M, K.) So in the phrase laqiYa wayosFA He found, or met with, or experienced, what he desired; (M, K;) accord. to an explanation given by IAar; so that it means much: but in one place he says that this phrase signifies he found, &c., what he did not desire. (M.)
